title: Assessment Examination
shortDescription: Classify portraits as Trust or Threat, then follow the examination when its orderly test screens give way to case-file text.

image.alt: Grainy face with dark eyes above the Assessment Examination title

seo.title: Play Assessment Examination: Trust or Threat Guide
seo.description: Play Assessment Examination and learn when to classify a portrait or read a case file. Get help with the response buttons, fullscreen and browser loading.

content.heading: A job application that asks for your judgment

blocks.text: Assessment Examination is a short psychological horror game built around an employment-style evaluation. You are applying to the Authenticity Assessment Department, and the examination turns that ordinary administrative setup into an uncomfortable exercise in judging what is in front of you. Its restrained interface makes the difference between an orderly test and a disturbing interruption feel unusually sharp.

This is a seated, screen-focused experience rather than a game about searching a house or running from an enemy. Attention matters more than movement: read the prompt, examine the image, then select an answer. Give the picture and the instruction separate moments of attention so that an unnerving detail does not make you overlook what the current question actually asks.

Allow around ten to fifteen minutes for the examination itself, with additional time for the browser build to download. An uninterrupted first attempt makes the changing presentation easier to follow. A line of dialogue or a brief shift on screen can connect two questions that otherwise look similar, so the quiet moments deserve as much attention as the obvious disturbances.

blocks.alt: An examination question with three visible response labels
blocks.caption: Read each question and its available responses before clicking.

content.heading: Read the label before judging the face

blocks.text: The central assessment asks you to distinguish between trust and threat. Treat those as the two available judgments rather than as attack and defence moves. Look at the whole image before moving to a choice. Notice expression, facial proportions and presentation together; do not turn one detail, such as an exaggerated smile, into a rule that replaces looking at the rest of the picture.

A practical rhythm is to read, inspect, decide and click once. Then wait for the interface to acknowledge the selection or continue. Repeated clicking makes it harder to tell which question received your answer, especially when successive screens share the same arrangement. If a picture changes while your pointer remains over a button, stop and read the new instruction before making another judgment.

You do not need to reveal personal information or prove something about your real judgment. The application is a fictional horror scenario. Responding to the presentation is the activity, and uncertainty is part of its effect. A single unnerving image is not a reason to stop interpreting all later prompts individually or to assume that an entire run can be reduced to selecting the same label.

blocks.alt: A portrait beside separate trust and threat buttons
blocks.caption: Judge the displayed portrait before choosing trust or threat.

content.heading: When the examination changes its pace

blocks.text: The assessment can give way to a case-file page with personal fields and narrative text. That change calls for reading rather than another judgment about a portrait. Follow the current text when the format shifts instead of expecting every screen to require the same classification. Let the sequence unfold before treating the absence of the familiar answer layout as a fault.

Separate slow presentation from a frozen browser. If text, sound or imagery is still changing, the game is continuing to communicate. Stay with that sequence rather than refreshing immediately. If the entire image remains frozen and no visible control responds, check the browser instead. Treating those as different problems prevents an intentional pause from becoming an unnecessary restart.

For the first playthrough, discover the structure before trying to optimise it. An answer list can reveal what somebody selected, but it also removes the uncertainty that makes the assessment distinctive. Finish a run, remember the moments that changed your expectations, and then decide whether a second pass would help you understand them.

blocks.alt: A grainy group photograph with black bars obscuring the eyes
blocks.caption: The examination can change from answer controls to unsettling imagery.

content.heading: Set up the examination before the unsettling parts

blocks.text: Use a mouse or another precise pointing device for the response buttons. You do not need a movement-key layout to begin. The F key toggles the game's fullscreen mode, which can make text and images easier to follow. The surrounding player provides separate view controls; use one method at a time so that you know which control returns you to the page.

Set a comfortable volume before the assessment builds tension. Sound contributes to the atmosphere, but excessive loudness does not improve your ability to follow the questions. Lower or mute it if you need a break. Disturbing images and psychological horror describe the experience more usefully than a promise that everyone will find it equally mild or frightening.

A desktop or laptop offers the clearest combination of readable text and precise pointer input. A small phone display can compress the picture and answer labels together. Enlarging the player may help readability, but that alone does not establish complete touch compatibility. If the choices are awkward to reach on a phone, a computer is a more practical option than repeated small-screen tapping.

content.heading: Why the first download can take time

blocks.text: The browser edition loads a substantial game package before the examination begins. A progress display or a dark surface at the start can therefore be a download stage rather than the first question. Give the first load time to finish, especially on a slower connection. Opening several copies only adds competing downloads and makes the original problem harder to identify.

If the player reports a timeout, retry once and watch whether the next attempt progresses. If the same failure returns, check the connection and use an up-to-date browser. The game relies on a browser graphics runtime; a restricted device, unavailable graphics acceleration or blocked game assets can prevent it from starting even when this page opens normally.

A completed page load does not prove that the examination has started. Look for the assessment display and a responsive control. An error document, an indefinitely empty area or a permanent loading indicator should not be mistaken for a fictional event. Resolve that problem before starting a run. Refreshing a working examination interrupts the current sequence, so reserve it for an actual failure.

content.heading: Make the first run easy to follow

blocks.text: On each portrait screen, read the label before putting the pointer over an answer. Once you have chosen, click once and look back at the display. If a case file replaces the portrait, switch to reading its fields and narrative. Reusing the previous screen’s clicking pattern can make you miss the change in what the examination is asking you to do.

When a moment surprises you, identify what changed: image, wording, sound or pace. That gives you a concrete detail to think about later without requiring an elaborate explanation while the game is unfolding. Useful observations describe the presentation. They do not automatically assume that every unusual event means the last answer was incorrect.

On a second run, compare a small number of decisions and note the response you actually see. A different selection is not proof of a different ending. Keep a distinction between the answer you changed, the presentation that followed and any interpretation you made afterward; that is more useful than treating an unsupported answer chart as a scoring system.

content.heading: Choose this when you want uneasy observation

blocks.text: Assessment Examination fits the part of Suzy Says that puts pressure on interpreting an apparently simple instruction. The physical demand is different: this examination centres on reading and judging a screen, while Suzy's mat-based tasks make movement part of the uncertainty. Here, the uncomfortable decision occupies the centre of the experience.

Please Answer Carefully offers another ordinary interface that becomes threatening, with a more personal survey framing. Last seen online instead asks you to investigate an old computer and connect clues. Choose by the action you want next: respond to questions, inspect pictures or investigate files. None uses the examination's labels as a universal set of controls.

content.heading: Follow the examination interface

blocks.title: Assessment Examination: follow the examination interface
blocks.description: Watch image judgments give way to case-file text. Read the changed screen before expecting another portrait choice. This complete recording contains later story details.

title: Please Answer Carefully
shortDescription: Answer a questionnaire using checkboxes, single choices and a slider as its questions turn toward increasingly personal subjects.

image.alt: Please Answer Carefully title and red continuation arrow on its survey screen

seo.title: Play Please Answer Carefully: Survey Controls
seo.description: Play Please Answer Carefully and work through checkboxes, response circles and the hours slider. Find the next prompt without revealing the survey ending.

content.heading: An ordinary questionnaire becomes uncomfortable

blocks.text: Please Answer Carefully begins as a modest online questionnaire. You select responses about everyday internet habits, move through a familiar form and gradually find the questions becoming less impersonal. The horror lives in that change of relationship: a screen that initially asks for information starts to feel as though it expects something from you. There is no house to explore or enemy to outrun. Your attention stays on wording, choices and sound.

The game is a short text-based experience by litrouke. A first visit normally fits into a few minutes, although taking time over every change can make it longer. Its instructions allow roughly five to ten minutes. It works best when you can read without interruption, because the layout sometimes matters as much as the question. Treat it as a compact story told through a form rather than a personality quiz that will give you a useful real-world assessment.

Stalking is the central content concern. The personal tone and eerie audio can be uncomfortable even without an action sequence. The opening menu includes a content warning, so read that before beginning if this theme is difficult for you. You can also lower or mute the sound; completing a horror game is never a reason to ignore your own comfort.

content.heading: Select an option, then use the arrow

blocks.text: The title screen uses the same selection-and-continue language as the survey itself. Choose Begin game, then use the arrow that appears. Simply selecting the menu item is only the first part of the interaction. This is worth learning immediately, because the questionnaire repeatedly separates choosing a response from submitting it.

Language selection, the content warning and the credits are available from that opening menu. If the language is difficult to read, change it before starting the questionnaire. A menu choice can look selected while the page remains in place; look for the continuation arrow instead of selecting the same item repeatedly. The game is responding to a small form control, not asking you to double-click a desktop icon.

The introductory page includes an audio test. Use it to set a comfortable volume before the atmosphere becomes more intrusive. If the test is silent, check whether the browser tab or game sound is muted before proceeding. Audio can be important to the mood without being a reason to turn the volume unusually high. Begin at a moderate level and adjust down if necessary.

blocks.alt: Survey instructions with a red volume-test label and continuation arrow
blocks.caption: Set a comfortable volume before starting the questions.

content.heading: Checkboxes, response circles and the hours slider

blocks.text: The early questions teach three slightly different interactions. The device question allows multiple selections, so tick the options you want and then continue. The question about time spent online uses a slider. Later questions present a set of alternative responses. Read the instruction attached to each question instead of assuming every screen accepts the same kind of answer.

For the online-hours question, interact with the slider before looking for the next arrow. You can click a position on its track or move its handle to make a selection. Staring at the displayed scale does not submit an answer. If the arrow is absent at this point, first check whether you have actually interacted with the slider rather than treating the page as frozen.

For a question with response circles, choose one of the visible labels and then use the continuation arrow. Some controls may already have a default state, but the page can still wait for an interaction before revealing its next button. Click the label you intend to use instead of relying on a circle that looks filled. That is a more reliable way to distinguish a required selection from an unresponsive page.

The questions about messages deliberately separate work communication from personal communication. Read that distinction before responding. The important activity is noticing what changed between two similar-looking prompts, not finding a single answer that you can apply to every form. A quick glance can make two questions look identical even when one short phrase changes their meaning.

blocks.alt: Question one with multiple device checkboxes
blocks.caption: Device choices use checkboxes rather than a single response circle.

content.heading: A missing arrow does not always mean a broken game

blocks.text: If you cannot continue, first identify which kind of page is open. On an ordinary multiple-choice screen, interact with an answer label. On the hours question, interact with the slider. On a passage that is still revealing new words or choices, wait. These are different situations, and repeatedly clicking the empty area below the text will not solve all three.

Later parts of the questionnaire use timed text and delayed controls. The wording can arrive in pieces, and the available responses can change after the page first appears. Let the current sentence finish before deciding that there is nothing left to do. Pay attention to the form itself: a newly visible label, a changed response or a continuation control can be the next event.

Avoid holding down the mouse button or rapidly clicking where the next arrow usually sits. A timed change can place a different control under the pointer. Wait for a stable, visible choice, select it and then continue once. If everything genuinely stops changing and the intended control remains unresponsive, a reload is a browser-recovery step, but it can also interrupt your current attempt.

content.heading: Notice what the form asks you to accept

blocks.text: The questionnaire becomes more unsettling when its polite administrative style stops matching the substance of its demands. Read both parts of a prompt: the instruction that tells you how to respond and the statement you are responding to. Those can pull your attention in different directions. Recognising that tension is more useful than rushing to produce what looks like a successful survey response.

Some later choices provide less freedom than the first screens suggest. That narrowing is part of the story's pressure. Do not assume an unusual set of labels is a browser glitch merely because it no longer resembles a normal questionnaire. At the same time, the character's insistence is fictional. You are not required to agree with it outside the game or to carry any instruction away from the screen.

A replay is useful when you want to compare the wording around a particular answer. Change one response and read the next passage closely. That comparison can show a visible difference without telling you how every earlier answer affects the conclusion. Keep the final reveal for the end of your own run if you want the questionnaire’s change of tone to unfold gradually.

content.heading: Keep the text and the controls in view

blocks.text: A mouse is the simplest way to handle this questionnaire's labels and slider. Keep enough of the player visible to see the question and the continuation arrow together. If the text feels cramped, enlarge the player before answering rather than repeatedly changing the view while a timed passage is appearing. This is a reading interface, so legibility matters more than filling the screen with decorative space.

On a small display, watch for controls below the question before assuming they are missing. Changing the player's view can help, but it does not guarantee that every phone/browser combination handles the slider or text layout equally well. If selecting a label is unreliable, try a larger display and a precise pointer. Do not mistake a difficult target for a secret puzzle.

If the sound disappears while the text continues, check the game and tab volume rather than restarting immediately. If the entire game fails to load, use the player's retry control and check the connection. Avoid clearing browser data simply to repair a missed click: a wrong interaction and a broken load are different problems, and restarting is a larger interruption than selecting the correct visible control.

content.heading: Continue with another kind of unsettling interface

blocks.text: The survey rewards attention to small wording changes. Device choices may allow several selections, while a later prompt asks for one frequency or a response on each agreement row. Before continuing, check the current question’s subject and the input it expects. A familiar form layout can conceal a new distinction, such as work messages versus personal messages.

Assessment Examination moves the decision toward judging images, while last seen online opens the interface into a computer full of clues. Both offer a different next task after the survey. Choose image assessment when you want another focused series of judgments, or file investigation when you would rather explore and connect information at your own pace.

content.heading: Watch the questionnaire change

blocks.title: Please Answer Carefully: watch the questionnaire change
blocks.description: Compare device checkboxes with frequency options and agreement scales as the questions grow more personal. The complete recording reveals later questions and the conclusion.

title: last seen online
shortDescription: Investigate an old computer through chat histories, pictures and locked files. Match each password clue to the field that actually needs it.

image.alt: Glitched portrait with the last seen online title

seo.title: Play last seen online: Passwords and Desktop Guide
seo.description: Play last seen online and connect desktop clues without a solution list. Separate login and archive codes, uncover overlapping windows and follow new prompts.

content.heading: A second-hand computer with a life inside it

blocks.text: last seen online begins with a computer bought at a garage sale. Instead of wiping it, you turn it on and step into the traces of another person's life. Files, chat histories and desktop programs become the rooms of an escape game. The central activity is investigation: open something, read what it reveals and connect that information to a lock or question elsewhere.

This is the game by qwook and sochinstudio. Its old desktop and the world connected to it are a different experience from other games sharing the same name. The appeal lies in treating a familiar computer interface as a space that can conceal both ordinary memories and disturbing discoveries. You need curiosity and a willingness to revisit clues, rather than a list of facts gathered outside the game.

Read the opening warning before continuing. Psychological horror and distressing themes make this unsuitable for children or anyone who finds such material difficult. You can follow the early investigation without knowing where the story ends. Keeping final scenes and complete puzzle solutions for later preserves the pleasure of discovering why an apparently mundane file matters.

blocks.alt: An in-game portrait decorated with pink hearts
blocks.caption: Personal images give the old computer a history beyond its files and locks.

content.heading: Treat each program as a different kind of clue

blocks.text: Begin by reading the login hint and looking for the information it describes. A useful password hint is a request for particular pieces of knowledge, not permission to guess random words indefinitely. If it points to more than one detail, identify all of those details before submitting another attempt. Revisit the hint whenever your candidate matches only part of its wording.

Once inside the desktop, explore the programs with different expectations. The buddy list holds conversations and relationships. The music player holds a playlist and audio. A protected archive presents a separate lock, and the file browser gives access to pictures and folders. None should be treated as a decorative shortcut simply because it resembles an old real-world application.

Read a conversation far enough to understand who is speaking and what they are discussing. An old message about an attachment can matter to an archive, while a remark about a program or image can tell you where to look next. Keeping the speaker and subject together is more useful than collecting isolated numbers without knowing what they refer to.

If several windows obscure each other, close or move the ones that are not part of the current question. The desktop behind them is also a visible part of the game. A cluttered screen can hide information even when the relevant file is already open. Before deciding that a clue is absent, make the working area readable and examine how its pieces relate.

Several pictures can overlap on the desktop: a front window titled IMG004.jpg can obscure IMG003.jpg and lawson.jpg behind it. Before clicking, identify which title bar belongs to the image you want. Work with that window rather than assuming every visible corner belongs to the front picture. The desktop background remains another part of the scene, so rearranging your attention between windows and background is more useful than opening the same picture repeatedly.

blocks.alt: LoseAmp music-player window with a green playlist and playback controls
blocks.caption: Programs have different jobs; distinguish a playlist from chat or an archive lock.

content.heading: Keep the login and the archive lock separate

blocks.text: The computer login and the protected photo archive are not the same lock. Solving the first does not mean its answer belongs in every later password field. The archive interface asks for a four-digit code. That tells you what kind of answer to seek, and it prevents a common wrong turn: carrying a name-based login answer into a numeric archive prompt.

When an archive rejects a candidate, the useful next step is to review the clue chain. Did you identify the right items? Did you arrange them in the order the clue implies? Did you enter the requested number of digits? Changing a digit without a reason produces little information. Returning to a message or picture can show which part of your interpretation needs attention.

The desktop's music, conversations and imagery should be considered together. If a message directs attention toward music or a visual arrangement, inspect those particular elements rather than searching unrelated folders indefinitely. Separate selecting the relevant items from deciding their order. Those are two different tasks, and getting one right does not automatically solve the other.

You do not need specialist computer knowledge to reason through these interfaces. Treat the archive as a puzzle within the story, not as an invitation to extract a real file or install another program. Work with the visible controls and clues the game provides. If a procedure seems to require leaving the game to obtain somebody's private information, reconsider the clue before following that assumption.

content.heading: Read feedback when the setting changes

blocks.text: The investigation does not stay confined to ordinary folders. When it leads into Other World, continue using the same habit of reading the response to each action. A newly opened location can change what an interaction means. Do not assume every object is another password field merely because the opening puzzles involved a computer.

A black OtherCorp screen presents a different input task from the photo windows. Its InviteCode field sits with Continue and Back controls. Read that field label before typing: an invitation-code prompt is not the earlier desktop login or the protected archive simply because all three accept text. Check which screen is active and what kind of information it requests before reusing an old answer.

Some later interactions distinguish a brief press from holding a control. When nearby text draws attention to duration or repeated sounds, examine how the object responds to that difference. A click and a hold are separate actions. Repeating quick clicks will not demonstrate what a longer interaction does, so change the input deliberately and compare the visible or audible feedback.

Pay attention to partial feedback. A message that something changed does not necessarily mean the entire obstacle is solved. Pause and inspect the object again. If a mechanism has several parts, keep track of which action altered which part before restarting the whole sequence. This gives you a way to build on progress instead of treating every incomplete result as a complete failure.

Read instructions for a group of objects as carefully as individual clues. A requirement about order is different from a requirement about quantity. If one object needs repeated attention, selecting every object once may leave the sequence incomplete. Work out what the wording asks you to vary, then watch for the explicit response that marks progression. Exact sequences are best left until you have tried interpreting the clue yourself.

content.heading: Make a small clue trail instead of a pile of guesses

blocks.text: For a first run, keep notes in three columns: obstacle, related clue and attempted action. An archive entry might mention its required format, a conversation that discusses the attachment and the code you tried. A later mechanism might instead need a nearby inscription and an input pattern. The goal is to preserve relationships, not transcribe every line of dialogue.

When stuck, return to the nearest unanswered question. If the game asks for a numeric archive code, your immediate task is to identify numbers and their order. If it presents several objects governed by a shared instruction, the task is to apply that instruction to the group. Wandering between all open puzzles can feel active while leaving the actual missing step untouched.

Record what you changed after an unsuccessful attempt. For a code field, that may be the candidate and the clue you used; for a sequence, it may be which object you selected and in what order. Keep the failed attempt beside the obstacle it belongs to. Otherwise a discarded login guess can easily get mixed into your notes for a different lock.

blocks.alt: A desktop chat window with colored names and blue response links
blocks.caption: Read the conversation before choosing a reply or recording a clue.

content.heading: Adjust the computer without erasing the investigation

blocks.text: The settings include separate master, sound-effect and music volume controls. That distinction matters in a game where a playlist and other audio can help communicate a clue. If music is inaudible while effects still play, check the music setting as well as the browser tab volume. Raising the master control alone may not solve a separately muted music channel.

Choose a readable language before working through long conversations. The game has community translations, but an older video in another language can use different wording or an earlier visual style. Match the visible objects and the meaning of a clue rather than expecting every label or portrait to be identical to a recording.

Be careful with the option to restart from the beginning. It is a deliberate way to begin again, not a routine fix for a password rejected by a working puzzle. If you want to preserve progress, leave that control alone. Browser privacy settings or blocked third-party storage can also affect whether an embedded game retains state, so do not assume progress is permanently backed up merely because you have reached a later room.

After finishing, the credits include a replay control near their end. Scroll through them before clearing browser data to start another attempt. A fresh run is most useful when you want to revisit an earlier conversation or compare how a clue was introduced. It is less useful as a first response to an obstacle whose surrounding information you have not yet read.

content.heading: Separate a puzzle problem from an input problem

blocks.text: The desktop includes typing as well as pointing. Click the intended password field before entering text, and check that the characters actually appear there. If keys affect the surrounding webpage instead, return focus to the player and field. An empty field after typing is an input-focus problem; a visible rejected answer is a puzzle result. Those need different next steps.

A larger display makes overlapping windows, small labels and visual clue relationships easier to read. Touch input is listed for the game, but a phone still offers less room for comparing windows and handling precise targets. If a particular drag or text entry is awkward, use a computer with a mouse and keyboard instead of interpreting the difficulty as part of the mystery.

If the game never reaches its own opening interface, check the connection and retry the player before investigating passwords. If it has loaded and the problem concerns a particular lock, use the clue trail rather than repeatedly reloading. The distinction keeps a technical recovery step from unnecessarily interrupting an otherwise functioning investigation.

content.heading: Follow the desktop investigation

blocks.title: last seen online: follow the desktop investigation
blocks.description: Watch overlapping picture windows and the change to an invite-code screen. Notice which window and input label are active. The full recording reveals puzzle solutions and later scenes.

title: The Open House
shortDescription: Navigate a virtual property tour, remember its room labels and compare the sales presentation with what the house shows you.

image.alt: The Open House property-tour cover showing a house and diagonal real-estate banner

seo.title: Play The Open House: Rooms and Tour Controls
seo.description: Play The Open House and find your way through the virtual property tour. Read room labels and Information panels, with help for the browser build loading.

content.heading: A house tour that changes its tone

blocks.text: The Open House turns a familiar piece of online browsing into a short psychological horror game. Instead of arriving as an armed investigator, you enter a polished virtual property presentation. The apparent job is ordinary: look around a house, examine its rooms and understand what is being offered. That comfortable framing matters. A property tour encourages you to trust labels, interfaces and the person guiding the visit, so a change in those things feels different from a monster appearing in a place that already looked dangerous.

Approach the opening as a tour rather than a speed challenge. Notice the relationship between the sales presentation and the rooms it describes. A neat piece of interface text can tell you where the tour wants your attention, while the image may invite you to look elsewhere. The interest lies in that tension between a reassuring wrapper and an increasingly uncomfortable visit. You do not need knowledge of a film series, another horror game or real-estate terminology to understand the starting situation.

blocks.alt: The front exterior of the house in The Open House virtual tour
blocks.caption: Begin by recognizing the property before moving through its rooms.

content.heading: Get comfortable with the tour interface

blocks.text: Start the player and wait until the property presentation is ready before trying to move through it. Once the game has focus, use the controls shown inside its own frame. The Open House is an exploration experience, but that does not mean every view behaves like a conventional first-person shooter. Read a control prompt before holding movement keys or clicking the edge of the screen repeatedly. The useful question is whether the current view offers a route, an inspection action or a piece of information to read.

Make one deliberate input and give the scene time to respond. That makes it easier to connect an action to its result, particularly when a transition changes both the viewpoint and the available interface. If you click several directions while a new view is arriving, you can lose track of where you entered and which part of the room you have actually examined. A small pause at a doorway is often more useful than rapid random navigation, because the building is the subject of the game rather than a corridor to rush through.

blocks.alt: Kitchen view with a bright tour navigation marker and an information tab
blocks.caption: Notice the tour marker and information tab before choosing the next view.

content.heading: Keep track of rooms instead of wandering in circles

blocks.text: Use the rooms as landmarks. Remember where a doorway led, what was visible near an entrance and which route brought you back to a familiar space. You do not need a precise architectural drawing. A simple sequence such as entrance, connecting room and return route is enough to distinguish a new area from another angle on somewhere you already visited. When you are unsure, retrace one known connection before taking another unexplored route. That is a clearer method than repeatedly choosing whichever direction looks brightest.

Inspect the full available view before deciding a room has nothing else to offer. A tour image can hold information above, below or beside the most obvious doorway. Keep the interface and the room itself separate in your attention: a navigation marker is a way to change position, while a detail inside the room may be there to explain the current situation. If the game asks you to examine or revisit a place, return with that specific task in mind. Simply passing through a room again is not the same as checking what the new instruction asks you to inspect.

blocks.alt: Guest bathroom view labeled in the upper corner of the tour
blocks.caption: Room labels and fixtures help you recognize where the tour has taken you.

content.heading: Read changes in context

blocks.text: The horror works best when you remember what a normal part of the tour looked like. Look at the room, then read what the presentation is asking you to do, and only then decide on the next input. If something familiar has changed, compare its position, appearance or meaning with your earlier impression. You do not have to identify every decorative object. Focus on details that affect the visit: where you can go, what the interface calls a place and whether the next requested action still fits an ordinary property inspection.

An unsettling image and a technical failure are not automatically the same thing. The game is deliberately atmospheric, and its presentation can become less comfortable as it progresses. Before refreshing a dark or strange scene, check whether the interface still responds and whether a new prompt or route is present. Conversely, a browser error message, a frozen loading indicator or a missing game frame belongs to a different problem. Separating these cases prevents you from restarting a working scene just because the story has stopped feeling welcoming.

The living-room view gives you a clear example of how to divide your attention: blue walls and a fireplace belong to the pictured property, while an Information area sits below the scene. Read the information without forgetting to inspect the room itself. Later, a view labeled Hall 2F can present distorted colors rather than the clean sales image you first encountered. Keep the location label in mind when the image becomes strange. You can recognize that you are still navigating the tour without assuming that every visual change is a browser crash or a new movement system.

content.heading: Choose the next clear action

blocks.text: When you lose your place, narrow the problem to the current screen. What is the last instruction you read? Which room or part of the property does it concern? What input is available now? Answer those three questions before searching every other room. This keeps a small uncertainty from turning into a full restart. It also protects the pacing: the tour can build tension from waiting and looking, whereas constant clicking makes it harder to notice how the presentation is changing.

If you have lost your place, return to a room whose label you recognize and compare it with the last instruction. Use that point to retrace one route rather than clicking through every doorway again. Check the Information area when the presentation gives you a new task, then inspect the relevant room. A second visit is useful when you know what you are returning to examine.

content.heading: If the browser version does not start

blocks.text: The Open House uses a Unity WebGL browser build. A blank frame that never reaches the tour can therefore be a loading or browser-compatibility issue rather than a mystery to solve inside the house. Let the initial game data finish arriving, keep the game tab active during startup and avoid repeatedly reopening the player while it is still working. If the frame reports an error, read that message before retrying. The size of the surrounding page does not indicate whether the game itself has finished loading.

If a retry still cannot reach the opening presentation, try a different current desktop browser. This is a more useful comparison than changing several unrelated browser settings at once, because the game itself warns of WebGL differences between browsers. A laptop or desktop also gives the tour more room for its interface than a narrow phone display. Do not expect a touch screen to reproduce an unconfirmed desktop input scheme. If a control lies outside the visible game area, enlarge the player or rotate the device before assuming that the game has no way forward.

content.heading: A note before recording or streaming

blocks.text: The Open House can display the default system username during a segment. If you are recording the game, think about that before you begin rather than discovering it while broadcasting. Use a recording setup in which a personal-looking name will not surprise you, and review footage before sharing it. This warning concerns the game presentation; it should not be read as a claim that this website can inspect your operating system or that every browser and desktop build exposes the same information in the same way.

Before sharing a recording, check that its frames do not expose the system username. An early property view can show the tour’s interface without revealing the late images that change its tone. A complete video reaches beyond that introduction, so expect it to show developments you may prefer to discover during your own visit.

content.heading: Questions before entering the house

items.question: Is The Open House a property-buying website?
items.answer: No. It is a short horror game built around a fictional virtual property tour. The sales presentation is part of that fiction, not an offer to purchase a real house.

items.question: Should I know the ending before I start?
items.answer: The opening is designed to make an ordinary tour feel gradually less comfortable. Start without late-game details if you want the contrast to work; use a full walkthrough only when you need help with a specific point.

items.question: What should I do if a room seems to repeat?
items.answer: Check the last instruction and the route you took. Compare the current view with your earlier visit before deciding whether you have returned to the same location, found a different angle or encountered a changed scene.

content.heading: Take the virtual property tour

blocks.title: The Open House: take the virtual property tour
